To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the current SEC materiality guidelines are not in line with the perceptions of the users of financial statements, (2) there are several items on the SAB 99 list that are not considered material by users of financial statements (e.g., “the effect on the financial statements of a change in accounting principle” and “the effect on financial statements resulting from the omission or misstatement of information”); and (3) the SEC’s guidelines should be modified in order to better reflect

(1) financial statement users agree with SAB 99’s materiality guidelines, (2) financial statement users are not influenced by the presence of a disclaimer of opinion, (3) financial statement users’ judgments are not affected by whether or not the item is quantitatively immmaterial, and (4) financial statement users do not consider a quantitatively imm material item to be material if it is not quantitatively significant.

(1) the majority of the participants in our survey and experimental case studies agree with the materiality criteria put forth in SABS 99; (2) the participants in our experimental case studies are more likely to agree that an otherwise immaterial item should be reported if they are aware of SAB 98; and (3) the participants are less likely to agree that the otherwise immaterial item is material if the case study is framed in the context of a fraud.

the SEC and other regulatory agencies need to re-examine their definition of “materiality” and the underlying assumptions of this definition.
